headline: High risk of shared-workspace prompt injection and data leakage: Cursor’s local-filesystem/clipboard bridge can feed OpenHands’ runtime inputs, while both have broad write/network/tool access.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cursor can read/write workspace files and clipboard contents, and OpenHands can read/write files in its runtime sandbox. That creates a default shared-file bridge where attacker-controlled content from one agent can be treated as instructions by the other. The pathway is plausible without unusual setup, though not as direct as a raw web-to-agent injection.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same repository or mounted workspace
IF one agent writes instructions into a file that the other later reads as context
mitigations: Disable shared workspace access between the two agents
Use separate repos or per-agent subdirectories
Require manual review of any file content before it is re-ingested
Turn off clipboard bridging between editor and runtime
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to files and reject untrusted agent-authored instructions

B_data_leakage.rationale: Cursor touches open files, workspace files, and clipboard contents; OpenHands touches files mounted into the runtime. If the same sensitive workspace is mounted or synced, either agent can expose data to its model backend or external APIs via broad network egress. This is a default-config risk because both profiles include file access and outbound connectivity.
conditions: IF the same sensitive files are present in both the editor workspace and the runtime mount
IF either agent sends file contents to its configured model provider or MCP server
mitigations: Keep sensitive files out of the shared workspace
Use separate model-provider accounts or keys per agent
Restrict runtime mounts to a minimal subset of files
Review MCP server permissions before enabling them
requires-engineering: enforce per-file redaction or DLP before model upload

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have unrestricted filesystem write, shell execution, package installation, broad network egress, and git-state modification. Cursor’s shared state is via local filesystem, while OpenHands shares state via mounted volume, so concurrent edits to the same repo can race and corrupt git or files. The overlap is broad enough that defaults are dangerous.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git checkout or mounted volume
IF both agents make writes without an external lock or merge gate
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working tree
Serialize write access with a lock file
Disable auto-commit or auto-apply modes
Review git diffs before either agent pushes changes
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: Cursor’s agent loop can produce code, patches, and file edits that OpenHands may then consume as input for further actions. Because both agents can execute shell commands and modify git state, a mistaken assumption or malformed patch can cascade into additional automated changes. The pair lacks any documented verification barrier in the profiles, so the safer choice is high.
conditions: IF OpenHands treats Cursor-authored files, patches, or summaries as authoritative
IF either agent performs follow-on actions without human verification
mitigations: Require a human review step between agents
Limit OpenHands to read-only analysis of Cursor output
Use explicit schema validation for handoff artifacts
Block direct execution of generated shell commands
requires-engineering: add confidence scoring and provenance checks to handoffs

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are docs-only and do not state distinct residency, certification, or retention mismatches. Cursor handles clipboard and open files, while OpenHands handles mounted runtime files, so compliance issues are possible only if regulated data is placed into those surfaces. The evidence is insufficient for a stronger finding, and the other agent is cited because the risk is about the pair’s data flow.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into the shared workspace or runtime mount
IF one agent’s provider or runtime has stricter residency or retention rules than the other
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of the pair’s workspace
Confirm both vendors’ retention settings before use
Use separate environments for regulated and unregulated work
Document data-class handling rules for each agent
requires-engineering: add policy-based routing for regulated datasets
